A mathematical check that also rules out one proposed step

To send zero, use 000. To send one, use 111. The reader of the message chooses whichever bit appears most often.

Choose a starting bit, then flip one transmitted bit. The original is recovered. Flip two and the answer changes to the wrong original. This small example is different from the larger error-correcting code discussed in the research.

Choose a starting bit: zero or one. Flip one of the three bits, then a second. Watch the decoded answer.

Words used here
code
A rule for representing a message so that some errors can be detected or repaired.
bit
One binary digit: zero or one.
Read the fuller explanation

This bench uses a deliberately small repetition code. The bit zero is represented by three zeros, and one by three ones. A majority decoder repairs one flipped bit. With two flips it confidently returns the wrong original bit.

That is the whole declared example. It explains why redundancy, allowed words, distance and error assumptions matter. It is not the ternary Golay code studied in the source, and it supplies no bridge from a code to a physical or biological mechanism.

The source’s arithmetic audit also retains an obstruction: a proposed intrinsic ordering does not follow from the named symmetry. A successful calculation and a failed promotion can live together in the same workshop.
